entities.name: Dutch East India Company
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Dutch East India Company (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, VOC), chartered in 1602 and dissolved in 1799, was the world's first multinational corporation and the most powerful trading company in history — operating 4,785 ships, employing 1 million people, paying 18% annual dividends for almost 200 years, and having a peak valuation estimated at $7.9 trillion in today's dollars (greater than Apple, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Facebook combined). The VOC pioneered financial instruments (stocks, bonds, dividends) that created modern capital markets.

The VOC's founding in 1602 merged six competing Dutch trading companies under state charter, granting it monopoly rights over Dutch trade with Asia, plus quasi-governmental powers: the right to wage war, negotiate treaties, mint coins, and establish colonies. The Amsterdam Stock Exchange (founded 1602 specifically for VOC share trading) is the world's first stock exchange. The VOC issued the world's first publicly traded shares, making speculative investment in distant trade accessible to ordinary citizens — creating financial capitalism's foundational instruments.

At peak (1640s-1660s), the VOC controlled access to the Spice Islands (Maluku, Indonesia), giving it monopoly over nutmeg, mace, cloves, and pepper — the world's most profitable commodities. The Batavia (Jakarta) headquarters became Southeast Asia's commercial hub. The VOC's 1619 massacre at Banda Islands (killing approximately 15,000 Banda islanders for nutmeg monopoly) is one of history's most extreme cases of commercial violence. The VOC's 1799 bankruptcy — from corruption, competition, and war — transferred its colonial assets to the Dutch government, creating the Dutch East Indies (modern Indonesia).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The VOC — the first multinational corporation, the first publicly traded stock, the first stock exchange — created financial capitalism's foundational instruments, and its $7.9 trillion peak valuation (greater than today's five largest companies combined) makes it the most economically powerful entity in history.
